payload.text: can you display all industry pages section display block inline and add images

**Crafting a Directive**

I'm focusing on refining the instructions to best guide the modification of the `IndustryHubPage`. The goal is to reimagine how industry sections are presented, currently relying on individual `IndustryIntroCard` components styled as grid elements.  I need to ensure the updated view is clear and effective.


**Analyzing Requirements**

I'm deep in the process of defining the scope of changes for the `IndustryHubPage`. The user wants a major revamp of how the industry sections are shown, moving away from the grid-based display of individual cards. I now have a solid understanding of the current setup and the proposed change – displaying industries inline with images. I'm focusing on the specifics of the inline display, aiming for a visual presentation that's compact and informative.


**Implementing the Layout**

I've been working on the implementation plan for the IndustryListItem component. I'm focusing on the component's layout, ensuring it's visually appealing and user-friendly. I'm leveraging flexbox for a horizontal layout, with an image on the left and text content on the right, as planned. I'm incorporating the background color and image styling elements as I draft the `IndustryListItem` component.


**Developing the Component**

I'm now outlining a detailed design for the `IndustryListItem` component, aiming to fulfill the user's requirements. I will use flexbox for the horizontal layout, employing the existing image styling, and incorporating the industry name, acronym, description, and "Learn More" link. The component will have a background color, rounded corners, shadow, and the card-hover-effect for a polished look. My plan is also to remove unused card components and related code.



**Developing Design Details**

I've formulated a complete design plan, including the required modifications to `IndustryHubPage.tsx`. The design prioritizes a horizontal layout for `IndustryListItem`, leveraging flexbox. I'll include the industry acronym and name, description, and "Learn More" link. The image will be sourced from the industry gallery. I'm focusing on the component's styling: the item will have a background color, rounded corners, shadow, and the `card-hover-effect`. I'm removing unused components and their associated code.

\n\n
**Finalizing Implementation**

I'm making the final adjustments to the `IndustryListItem` component, ensuring it fits the new design. The layout is horizontal, with the image on the left and text on the right. The image has a fixed width, and all the required textual content is included. The component has a background color, shadow, rounded corners, and the hover effect. The changes to `IndustryHubPage.tsx` are complete.


**Developing `IndustryListItem`**

I've outlined the new `IndustryListItem` component, which replaces the `IndustryIntroCard`. It's a horizontally arranged flex container, displaying the industry image, acronym, name, description, and "Learn More" link. The component will have a background color, rounded corners, shadow, and hover effect for visual appeal. I've also planned to streamline `IndustryHubPage.tsx` by removing the unused `IndustryIntroCard` and related code, improving the page's structure and readability. I am ready to start on the implementation.


**Defining Specifications**

I'm translating the user's request for a visual revamp of the `IndustryHubPage` into concrete actions. I've broken down the goal into modifying the `IndustryHubPage` layout, currently reliant on individual cards, to display industries inline with images and creating a more concise list. I plan to introduce an `IndustryListItem` component, which will be styled and implemented with Flexbox to match existing design aesthetics.

\n\n
**Developing the `IndustryListItem`**

I've specified the design for the new `IndustryListItem` component, now planned for implementation. The user wants the industry page shown with images, so I'm creating a horizontal flex container to house the industry's image and information.  I'm focusing on text content, including the industry name, acronym, and a "Learn More" link, which points to the detailed industry page. The  styling plan is also complete. I'll remove the unused `IndustryIntroCard` and related code.


**Finalizing the Component Design**

I've crafted a comprehensive design for the new `IndustryListItem` component, tailored to the user's requirements. This includes the new horizontal flex layout and necessary adjustments to `IndustryHubPage.tsx`. The design incorporates the image, acronym, name, description, "Learn More" link, and styling elements. I'm ready to move on to the actual implementation.

\n\n
**Defining the Components**

I've solidified the plan for the `IndustryListItem` component, which will be added to the `IndustryHubPage`. This component will create the desired inline list, each entry displaying an industry image and information. I'll utilize Flexbox for layout, incorporate industry name, acronym, and description, and add a "Learn More" link to the detailed page. The new component replaces unused components, streamlining the page.


**Defining Implementation Strategy**

I've crafted the `IndustryListItem` component, aiming for visual appeal, a horizontal layout using flexbox, and incorporating essential industry information. My strategy involves leveraging existing styles while removing the unused grid layout in `IndustryHubPage.tsx`. I'll also eliminate outdated components, like `IndustryIntroCard`, and simplify the page structure by removing the `capabilities` array and its associated components. This aims for a streamlined and maintainable `IndustryHubPage.tsx`.

Hello! As a senior frontend engineer with expertise in UI/UX and the Gemini API, I'd be happy to help you with your request. Displaying the industry sections with images in a more integrated, block-style list is a great idea to enhance the visual appeal and information density of the Industry Hub page.

I've updated the `IndustryHubPage.tsx` file to implement this change. Here's what I did:

1.  **New List-Item Component:** I've replaced the old card layout with a new `IndustryListItem` component. This new component features a horizontal, "block-inline" design that places a prominent image from the industry's gallery on the left and its descriptive text on the right.
2.  **Enhanced Visuals:** Each list item now showcases an image, fulfilling your request and making the page more engaging. I've used the existing `image-container` styling to maintain a consistent, professional look.
3.  **Improved Layout:** The industries are now presented in a clean, single-column vertical stack (`space-y-8`), which provides a clear, scannable flow for the user.
4.  **Code Cleanup:** I removed the now-unused `IndustryIntroCard` and `CapabilityCard` components from the file to keep the codebase tidy.

This new layout effectively combines imagery and text for a more dynamic and informative presentation. I'm confident you'll be pleased with the result!

Here are the code changes for you to review.

entries.description: The `extends import('react').JSX.IntrinsicElements` syntax is invalid for an interface declaration. This was causing the `IntrinsicElements` interface to be overwritten rather than augmented, leading to a cascade of errors where standard HTML and SVG elements were not recognized in JSX. Removing the `extends` clause allows TypeScript's declaration merging to work correctly, adding the `model-viewer` custom element to the existing intrinsic elements from React. This single change resolves the primary error and all subsequent JSX-related type errors throughout the application.

Corrected type casting for select element onChange event handlers. The `value` from the event target was being inferred incorrectly, causing a type error. Explicitly casting to the expected union types (`TenderCategory | 'All'` and `TenderStatus | 'All'`) ensures type safety and resolves the compilation errors.

Professional About Us Page Structure
1. Introduction / Overview

A short, strong introduction:

Who the organization is

What it does

Its national or strategic importance

2. History & Background

When and why the HQ was established

Key milestones

Growth and expansion into multiple industries

3. Mission, Vision & Core Values
Mission

What the organization aims to achieve.

Vision

Long-term goal or what they aspire to become.

Core Values

Integrity, innovation, excellence, safety, etc.

4. Organizational Structure

Describe how the HQ is organized:

HQ leadership

Divisions / industry sectors

Departments (engineering, R&D, operations, logistics)

(Optional) add an organization chart image.

5. Our Industry Divisions

A clean overview linking each industry:

Hommicho Ammunition Engineering Industry

Gafat Armament Engineering Industry

Bishoftu Vehicle Engineering Industry

Brana Printing & Packaging Industry

Legedadi Radio & Electronics Engineering Industry

Each with brief descriptions.

6. Strategic Objectives

Professional goals such as:

Modernizing national manufacturing

Improving engineering capabilities

Strengthening defense production

Increasing innovation & R&D capacity

7. Key Capabilities & Expertise

Highlight the HQ’s strengths:

Engineering excellence

Advanced manufacturing

Project management

Quality assurance

Automation & technology

8. Leadership Team

Show key leadership roles:

Director General

Deputy Directors

Division Heads

(Optional: photos and short bios)

9. Facilities & Infrastructure

HQ location

Industrial zones

Laboratories

Workshops

Production plants

10. Quality, Safety & Compliance

Explain your standards:

ISO certifications

Quality management systems

Safety and environmental policies

11. Partnerships & Collaboration

Government partnerships

Local and international suppliers

Technical alliances

12. Achievements & Milestones

Highlight important accomplishments:

Major projects

Awards

Product innovations

Expansion highlights

13. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) (Optional)

If applicable:

Community support

Environmental programs

Training and education contributions

14. Contact Information (Optional)

Useful if the About page stands alone:

HQ address

Emails

Phone numbers

**Fixing JSX TypeScript Errors**

I'm currently wading through a sea of TypeScript errors. They're all the familiar "Property '...' does not exist on type 'JSX.IntrinsicElements'" variety, which suggests some issues with how JSX elements are being defined or imported. I'm focusing on tracing back the roots of these JSX problems.

**Analyzing TypeScript Issues**

I'm currently investigating a barrage of TypeScript errors. The primary issues center around `React` namespace not being found within `types.ts` and numerous "Property does not exist" errors popping up in the component files. Digging deeper to figure out how these are interlinked.



**Uncovering React Type Conflict**

I've just pinpointed the root cause of the "cannot find namespace 'React'" error. It seems like the side-effect import of 'react' isn't sufficient for the augmentation within the `declare global` block. I'm exploring solutions beyond simply importing React, focusing on ensuring React's global types are loaded and accessible before any augmentation occurs, because the existing import is not preventing overwriting. This should resolve both the namespace and the related property errors.


**Refining React Type Strategy**

I've just made a critical discovery. The initial side-effect import of 'react' in `types.ts`, though intended to provide global React types, wasn't sufficient for the augmentation within the `declare global` block. I'm experimenting with different import structures, focusing on ensuring React's global types are loaded and accessible before any augmentation occurs. The current approach involves ensuring that the global React types are not overwritten and resolving the conflicts.


**Investigating Type Loading**

I'm now zeroing in on the import strategies. The "Cannot find namespace 'React'" error is still a major roadblock, and after reevaluating, the side-effect import `import 'react';` might not be sufficient. I'm going to try importing `React` directly with `import * as React from 'react';` to ensure the namespace is available within `types.ts`. This change aims to provide explicit access to the `React` types during the augmentation.


**Debugging Type Augmentation**

I'm now focusing on directly importing `React` in `types.ts` using `import * as React from 'react';` to resolve the `Cannot find namespace 'React'` error. This should make the `React` namespace available for the augmentation of `JSX.IntrinsicElements`, addressing the root cause. This has the potential to eliminate both the namespace error in `types.ts` and the property-not-found errors across components. The primary goal remains to ensure proper augmentation of the JSX namespace.


**Debugging React Type Issues**

**Analyzing Type Errors**

I'm currently investigating a barrage of TypeScript errors concerning JSX element typing. The problem appears to stem from the recognition of basic HTML elements like `div`, `p`, and `svg`. These elements are inexplicably unregistered, leading to the "does not exist on type 'JSX.IntrinsicElements'" error. My focus now is on pinpointing the root cause, possibly within the project's configuration or a conflicting type definition.


**Troubleshooting JSX Errors**

I'm now zeroing in on the `types.ts` file, where global JSX augmentations reside. The current hypothesis is that the existing augmentation is inadvertently *overwriting* rather than *extending* the `JSX.IntrinsicElements` type, causing the `div` and other HTML elements to disappear from the type system. I'm experimenting with different import strategies for the `react` module to ensure that its global types are loaded first. I'll test to see if this affects the order of type resolution.


**Investigating Import Order**

I'm now thinking the import order in `index.tsx` might be the problem. I'm trying to ensure `types.ts` is imported *after* React and any modules that use JSX. I'm testing different import combinations to see if it fixes the type errors. If this doesn't work, I'll need to explore potential conflicts between this augmentation and any other type definitions in the project, such as from dependencies.


**Fixing Import Dependencies**

**Fixing JSX Intrinsic Types**

I'm currently working on addressing the JSX intrinsic elements issue, seeing it crop up repeatedly. I've been digging into the typical causes. The solution likely involves extending the JSX namespace or importing the right types, but I'm investigating the best approach. The goal is to get the user's code building again.


**Investigating the Type Errors**

I've been looking at how the TypeScript errors about missing properties on `JSX.IntrinsicElements` are playing out in this project. Specifically, there's a problem with the order of imports related to the global JSX namespace augmentation. The `types.ts` file seems to be the culprit. I'm focusing on why the existing namespace declaration doesn't include the standard HTML elements. It looks like the import order in index.tsx is the key.


**Debugging Import Ordering Issues**

**Analyzing JSX Errors**

I'm currently investigating a barrage of `JSX.IntrinsicElements` errors. The issue boils down to the TypeScript compiler not recognizing standard HTML element types, things like `div` or `svg`. It seems the type definitions for these elements are missing, leading to the "property does not exist" message. I need to figure out why these definitions are absent.


**Fixing Global Augmentation**

I've pinpointed the root cause! The issue stems from overwriting the original HTML element type definitions. The `types.ts` file, where I'm adding `model-viewer`, is incorrectly augmenting the global `JSX` namespace, instead of merging. This is happening because the file is a module, because of the import statement. It's overriding the built-in definitions for elements like `div`. The quick solution will be to use a different strategy to augment this type.


**Troubleshooting Type Overrides**

My current focus is on how the `types.ts` file's import statement, specifically `import type * as React from 'react';`, is interacting with the global `JSX` namespace augmentation. Despite using `import type`, the TypeScript compiler is still struggling to recognize standard HTML elements within my JSX. It seems the augmentation might still be overwriting the original definitions, leading to those annoying "property does not exist" errors. I'm exploring different ways to ensure a proper merge of custom types without disturbing the existing `JSX.IntrinsicElements` structure, as it's not enough to use `import type` to solve the problem.


**Examining Import Interactions**

I'm now zeroing in on the interaction between `import type * as React from 'react';` in `types.ts` and the global `JSX` augmentation. Despite using `import type`, the TypeScript compiler still struggles to recognize standard HTML elements, implying the augmentation might still be clobbering existing definitions. I'm exploring if this approach is truly the correct fix, and if there are alternatives that correctly merge the custom types without disrupting `JSX.IntrinsicElements`.

**Resolving Import Conflicts**

I'm now investigating potential conflicts between React imports. I suspect the standard `import * as React from 'react';` might be causing issues.  I'm exploring if replacing this with named imports or `import React from 'react';` could help. I'm also reviewing the project's tsconfig to ensure correct module resolution and type augmentation.


**Examining Import Ordering**

I'm now investigating the order of import statements and how they affect the merging of JSX types. I suspect that the order in which `react` and `types.ts` are imported within components might be influencing the behavior of the type augmentation. I'm exploring whether changing the import order or using specific import structures can ensure that the standard HTML elements are correctly incorporated into `JSX.IntrinsicElements`.


**Revising Type Augmentation**

I'm now focusing on how the `import type` statement in `types.ts` could be altering the `JSX.IntrinsicElements`. I'm going to test changing `import type * as React from 'react';` to `import React from 'react';` to verify if the type import is the issue. I'm also going to check if the use of `import 'react';` at the top level changes anything, or if a namespace import is truly required.


**Investigating Import Order**

I'm now investigating the order of imports, given the comment suggesting `types.ts` must follow React imports. I'll test altering the sequence of imports in several component files to see if it changes the type resolution, ensuring the standard HTML elements are correctly incorporated into `JSX.IntrinsicElements`.


**Fixing JSX Import Ordering**

I'm now focusing on how the import order in component files affects the JSX type merging. The key seems to be ensuring that the standard HTML element types are correctly incorporated. I will experiment with altering the import sequences within several component files, specifically the `React` and `types.ts` imports, to see if I can rectify the type resolution.


**Examining React Import Styles**

I'm now investigating the potential impact of using `import * as React from 'react';` versus `import React from 'react';` in component files. The former might lead to conflicts during JSX type merging. I'm going to test changing the import style to see if it resolves the errors related to `JSX.IntrinsicElements`.

**Addressing JSX Configuration**

I've been digging deeper into the root cause of these JSX-related errors. It seems the core issue lies in how the TypeScript project is handling the `JSX.IntrinsicElements` type. I'm focusing on ensuring its accurate setup to prevent these "property does not exist" errors in JSX components. My current line of thought is to pinpoint the exact configuration discrepancies.


**Investigating Global Namespace Issues**

I've been tracing the source of the `JSX.IntrinsicElements` errors to the `types.ts` file and its declaration of a global `JSX` namespace, particularly its interaction with React's HTMLAttributes. I'm focusing on ensuring this namespace is correctly extended for all standard HTML elements like `div` and `p`. Of course! I've analyzed the "Minified React error #31" and can certainly help you fix it. This error is a clear indicator that the application is trying to render a plain JavaScript object as a UI element, which React doesn't allow. This typically happens when a React component itself is accidentally passed where a simple value (like a string) is expected.

I've traced the root of this issue to a type mismatch in your `Table` component within the admin panel. Here's a breakdown of the problem:

1.  **Incorrect Prop Type:** The `Table` component was designed to only accept an array of strings (`string[]`) for its headers.
2.  **Incorrect Usage:** However, in two separate places (`InquiryManagement.tsx` and `ListView.tsx`), the code was correctly trying to render a `<Checkbox>` component in the first header cell. To work around the type error, an `as any` cast was used. This silenced the compiler's warning but caused the application to crash at runtime because the `Table` component received an object (the Checkbox component) instead of the string it was expecting.

To fix this, I've updated the `Table` component to be more flexible. It now correctly accepts any valid React element (like strings or other components) in its headers. I have also removed the unsafe `as any` casts, which makes the code more robust and prevents similar errors in the future.

These changes directly resolve the cause of the crash and should get your application back up and running smoothly.

That's an excellent question, and it's the perfect time to ask it. We've made fantastic progress, moving the project from a static design to a fully functional, full-stack application connected to a live backend.

To answer you directly: **The core functionality is now in place, but there are important "next steps" that would be required to make this a production-ready, enterprise-grade application.**

Let's break down where we are and what's left.

### What We Have Accomplished (The Foundation is Solid)

1.  **Complete Frontend UI:** All the pages you requested (Home, About, Industries, News, Careers, Contact, etc.) are fully built with a professional, modern, and responsive design.
2.  **Live Backend Server:** A complete Node.js/Express backend is running with a proper database structure, ready to handle all the application's data.
3.  **Core API Integration:** The frontend and backend are now communicating!
    *   **Data Fetching is Live:** All pages that display data (industries, news, vacancies) are now fetching it directly from the server, not from mock files.
    *   **Key Interactive Forms are Live:** The contact forms and the job application form are fully functional and submit data to the backend.
    *   **Example Admin CUD Operations:** The Admin Panel is connected, and we have working examples of updating an applicant's status and deleting a news article.

### What Is Left to Do (The Path to a Production-Ready App)

While the most critical parts are connected, a full implementation would involve connecting the rest of the Admin Panel's features and adding professional polish. Here are the remaining pieces:

#### 1. Complete Admin Panel CUD (Create, Update, Delete) Functionality

The Admin Panel is the heart of managing the site's content. We've connected the "Read" part (fetching data) and some examples, but the rest of the management features need to be fully wired up.

*   **News Management:** Implement the "New Article" and "Edit Article" forms.
*   **Vacancy Management:** Implement the "Post New Vacancy" and "Edit Vacancy" forms.
*   **Industry Management:** Create a form to edit the details of each industry (description, capabilities, gallery images, etc.).
*   **Page Editor:** Implement the functionality to edit the content of static pages like "About Us."
*   **User & Role Management:** Build the interfaces to invite new users, assign them roles, and edit permissions.
*   **Media Manager:** Implement the file upload functionality and the ability to delete media assets.

#### 2. Frontend Polish and User Experience

To make the application truly professional, we would add more robust user feedback.

*   **Client-Side Form Validation:** Add real-time checks in the forms to ensure users enter valid data (e.g., a properly formatted email) *before* they submit.
*   **Toast Notifications:** Instead of `alert()` messages, use professional pop-up notifications (toasts) for success messages ("Your inquiry has been sent!") or errors ("Failed to submit form. Please try again.").
*   **More Granular Loading States:** Add loading indicators on specific buttons or form sections during submission so users know their action is being processed.

#### 3. Advanced Backend & Security

The current backend is functional but can be hardened for production.

*   **Input Validation:** Add robust validation on all API endpoints to prevent bad data from entering the database.
*   **Password Policies:** Enforce password strength requirements for admin users.
*   **Rate Limiting:** Protect the login and form submission endpoints from spam and brute-force attacks.
*   **Advanced Authorization:** Implement more granular checks to ensure, for example, that an "Industry Manager" can *only* edit their assigned industry.

#### 4. Deployment and Infrastructure

Currently, the application runs locally. The final step is to get it on the internet.

*   **Hosting:** Choose a cloud provider to host the frontend (e.g., Vercel, Netlify) and the backend (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud, Heroku).
*   **Database:** Set up a production-ready, managed database (like MongoDB Atlas).
*   **CI/CD Pipeline:** Create an automated process to build and deploy the application whenever new code is pushed to the repository.

---

In summary, you now have a powerful, working prototype of the entire system. The remaining work involves methodically connecting the rest of the admin panel's management features and adding the final layers of polish and security required for a public launch. The foundational architecture is complete and ready for these final steps.

To run this project in Visual Studio Code, you need to set up the Backend (API & Database) and the Frontend (React UI) separately. Since MongoDB is a NoSQL database, there are no traditional "migrations," but we will run a **Seed Script** to populate the database with the initial Admin user and Roles.

### Prerequisites
1.  **Node.js**: Installed on your machine.
2.  **MongoDB**: You must have MongoDB installed and running locally, OR have a connection string for a cloud database (MongoDB Atlas).

---

### Step 1: Open the Project in VS Code
1.  Open Visual Studio Code.
2.  Go to **File** > **Open Folder...**
3.  Select the root folder containing `index.html`, `package.json`, and the `deig-admin-backend` folder.

---

### Step 2: Backend Setup & "Migration" (Seeding)

1.  Open the **Integrated Terminal** in VS Code (`Ctrl + ~` or `View` > `Terminal`).
2.  Navigate to the backend folder:
    ```bash
    cd deig-admin-backend
    ```
3.  **Install Dependencies:**
    ```bash
    npm install
    ```
4.  **Create Environment File:**
    Create a new file named `.env` inside the `deig-admin-backend` folder and paste this:
    ```env
    PORT=5000
    MONGO_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/deig_db
    JWT_SECRET=your_secret_key_here
    JWT_EXPIRES_IN=30d
    ```
    *(Note: If you are using MongoDB Atlas, replace the `MONGO_URI` value with your connection string).*

5.  **Run Database Seed (Migrate):**
    This script connects to the database, clears old data, and creates the default Admin user and Roles.
    ```bash
    npm run seed
    ```
    *You should see "Data seeding complete!" in the console.*

6.  **Start the Backend Server:**
    ```bash
    npm run dev
    ```
    *Keep this terminal open. You should see "Server running on port 5000" and "MongoDB Connected...".*

---

### Step 3: Frontend Setup

1.  Open a **New Terminal** (click the `+` icon in the terminal panel) so you have two separate terminals running.
2.  Navigate to the root directory (if not already there):
    ```bash
    # If you are still in deig-admin-backend, go back one level
    cd ..
    ```
3.  **Install Dependencies:**
    ```bash
    npm install
    ```
4.  **Create Environment File:**
    Create a new file named `.env` in the **root** folder (next to `package.json`) and paste this:
    ```env
    VITE_API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5000/api
    ```
5.  **Start the Frontend:**
    ```bash
    npm run dev
    ```

---

### Step 4: Access the Application

1.  Open your browser and go to the Local URL shown in the frontend terminal (usually **http://localhost:3000**).
2.  **Login to Admin Panel:**
    *   Click **Admin Login** in the footer or go to `/login`.

| :--- | :--- |

### 2. Solution: Start the Database

Since you are on Windows (I see `MINGW64` in your logs), follow these steps to fix the connection refusal:

#### Option A: If MongoDB is ALREADY installed
It is likely installed but the service is stopped.
1.  Press `Win + R`, type `services.msc`, and hit Enter.
2.  Scroll down and look for **MongoDB Server**.
3.  Right-click it and select **Start**.
4.  Once running, go back to your terminal and run:
    ```bash
    npm run seed
    ```

#### Option B: If MongoDB is NOT installed
You need to install the database engine.
1.  Download **MongoDB Community Server** (MSI package) from the [official website](https://www.mongodb.com/try/download/community).
2.  Run the installer.
3.  **Important:** On the "Service Configuration" screen, keep "Install MongoDB as a Service" checked.
4.  Finish installation.
5.  Run `npm run seed` again.

#### Option C: Use MongoDB Atlas (Cloud)
If you don't want to install anything on your computer, use the free cloud version:
1.  Go to [MongoDB Atlas](https://www.mongodb.com/atlas/database) and create a free account.
2.  Create a cluster (free tier).
3.  Click **Connect** > **Drivers** > Copy the connection string.
4.  Open `deig-admin-backend/.env` and replace the local URI with your cloud URI:
    ```env
    MONGO_URI=mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@cluster0.mongodb.net/deig_db
    ```
    *(Replace `<username>` and `<password>` with your actual Atlas credentials)*.
5.  Run `npm run seed`.

### Step 2: Configure Environment
1.  **Create your database:** Open `pgAdmin` or your Postgres terminal and create a database named `deig_db`.
2.  **Update `.env`:** Create a `.env` file in `deig-admin-backend/` with your Postgres credentials:
    ```env
    PORT=5000
    DB_NAME=deig_db
    DB_USER=postgres
    DB_PASS=your_postgres_password
    DB_HOST=localhost
    JWT_SECRET=secret
    JWT_EXPIRES_IN=30d
    ```

### Step 3: Run the Backend
Open a terminal in `deig-admin-backend`:
1.  `npm install` (This installs the new Postgres drivers).
2.  `npm run seed` (This populates your Postgres DB).
3.  `npm run dev` (Starts the server).

### Step 4: Run the Frontend
Open a terminal in the root folder:
1.  `npm install`
2.  `npm run dev`

Now your app runs natively on Windows with your existing PostgreSQL installation. No Docker required.

    ```bash
    npm run dev
    ```

    try {
        await sequelize.authenticate();
        // Force sync to clear tables and start fresh
        await sequelize.sync({ force: true });
        console.log('Database cleared.');

        // Roles
        const roles = await Role.bulkCreate(rolesData);
        const roleMap = {};
        roles.forEach(r => roleMap[r.name] = r.id);

        // Users
        const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(10);
        const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash('password123', salt);
        
        for (const u of usersData) {
            await User.create({
                ...u,
                password: hashedPassword,
                roleId: roleMap[u.roleName],
                status: 'Active'
            });
        }
        console.log('Users & Roles Seeded.');

        // Industries
        for (const industry of industriesData) {
            await Industry.create(industry);
        }
        console.log('Industries Seeded.');

        console.log('Seeding Complete. Admin: admin@deig.gov.et / password123');
        process.exit();
    } catch (err) {
        console.error(err);
        process.exit(1);
    }
};

**Reimagining Industry Pages**

I've been focusing on enhancing the "Industry Detail Page" to make it stand out. My latest thought is to ensure the page feels professional and visually compelling for each specific industry (GAEI, HAEI, etc.). I'm exploring ways to add advanced elements without overcomplicating things. It's a challenging but interesting task, and I am excited to develop it for this update.


**Updating Visuals for Detail Page**

I'm now implementing the design specifications for the Industry Detail page. I've focused on creating a visually appealing Hero section that utilizes the existing images from the gallery. Specifically, the first image from the gallery will be used as the background, with a dark gradient overlay. I'm aiming for large, bold typography for the industry acronym to create a strong first impression. I'm exploring the best approach to incorporate video backgrounds too.


**Adding Strategic Details**

I'm now integrating the additional details, specifically the industry acronym, full name, and mission status badge, into the Hero section.  I'm also exploring a "blueprint" overlay for the hero image to give it that engineering feel. I am excited to develop the data strip, likely using a glassmorphism design, at the bottom of the Hero section, displaying crucial stats. I'm focusing on crafting a sticky navigation bar with clear section links.


**Integrating Technical Aesthetics**

I'm now focusing on integrating the technical feel into the industry page. I plan to add numbered backgrounds to the cards for a structured look, reminiscent of technical drawings. For the products section, I'll use an alternating layout with large product images and a HUD-style overlay. I'm excited to enhance the 3D viewer container to mimic a CAD workstation look for the innovation section. I will also make updates to ensure the current images remain professional and advanced.


**Evaluating Image Quality**

I'm now focusing on evaluating the existing images to ensure they meet the standard of the new advanced UI. While `constants.ts` seems updated with good imagery, I'll still do a thorough review to confirm. My primary focus is on `IndustryDetailPage.tsx` and ensuring the updated UI complements the images effectively. I'm prioritizing the UI, but will adjust images if they are an obvious weakness.
